title: EFFECTS OF INDOOR LIGHTING, GENDER, AND AGE ON MOOD AND COGNITIVE PERFORMANCE
central_proposition: Indoor lighting functions as an affective source, conveying emotional meanings that are differentiated by gender and age, which in turn influences cognitive performance.

concept_definitions.name: Warm white lighting
concept_definitions.definition: Lighting with a color temperature of 3000 Kelvin, described as 'more reddish'.

concept_definitions.name: Cool white lighting
concept_definitions.definition: Lighting with a color temperature of 4000 Kelvin, described as 'more bluish'.

concept_definitions.name: Delta mood score
concept_definitions.definition: A measure representing the change in mood over time, where a negative sign indicates a decrease and a positive sign indicates an increase.

argument_structure: The paper reviews existing literature on affect elicitation and environmental influences on emotion and cognition, highlighting gaps in direct lighting-mood research. It then proposes an experimental agenda based on the hypothesis that indoor lighting is an affect source that influences mood and cognition, with effects modulated by gender and age. The study presents an experiment testing these hypotheses, and the results are interpreted through the lens of socio-cultural conditioning and age-related cognitive declines.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The coloring quality (type of lamp) of indoor lighting is proposed to convey different emotional meanings and affective loadings to different genders and age groups. This is mediated by 'culturally embedded conceptions' and 'decoding rules' (Buck, 1984; Rapoport, 1982) that individuals retrieve from memory to interpret the emotional displays of the luminous milieu. These differential emotional appraisals then influence mood, which subsequently impacts ongoing cognitive performance.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Indoor lighting is an affective source, thus, a mood inducer, that could change mood in participants.
The mood elicited by the lighting will influence the ongoing cognitions.
Indoor lighting will have an effect on mood differentiated by gender, age, or both.
bridge_warrants: Connects environmental psychology (physical factors affecting affect/behavior) with cognitive psychology (emotion-cognition links, cognitive gerontology).
Connects lighting research (visual perception, chronobiology) with psychological effects of light (mood, cognition).

Utilizes Buck's (1984) 'decoding rule' and Rapoport's (1982) concept of 'different meanings' to explain how lighting's coloring quality conveys emotional meanings differentiated by gender and age, linking to socio-cultural context.
methodological_critiques: Previous studies on psychological effects of lighting are few and have largely failed to show direct effects of lighting on mood.
model_structure: The study implicitly tests a model where indoor lighting characteristics (type of lamp) interact with demographic variables (gender, age) to influence mood (positive, negative), which in turn affects cognitive performance (problem solving, memory tasks). Additionally, demographic variables (age) directly influence the perception of room light (brightness, coolness).
limitations: The interpretation of gender differences in short-term recall was noted as 'difficult to interpret' by the authors.
The link between mood preservation and problem-solving performance for younger females was stated as 'tentatively at least'.

paper_metadata.title: Emotion triggers executive attention: Anterior cingulate cortex and amygdala responses to emotional words in a conflict task
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Emotion triggers executive attention: Anterior cingulate cortex and amygdala responses to emotional words in a conflict task
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractCoherent behavior depends on attentional control that detects and resolves conflict between opposing actions. The current functional magnetic resonance imaging study tested the hypothesis that emotion triggers attentional control to speed up conflict processing in particularly salient situations. Therefore, we presented emotionally negative and neutral words in a version of the flanker task. In response to conflict, we found activation of the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and of the amygdala for emotional stimuli. When emotion and conflict coincided, a region in the ventral ACC was activated, which resulted in faster conflict processing in reaction times. Emotion also increased functional connectivity between the ventral ACC and activation of the dorsal ACC and the amygdala in conflict trials. These data suggest that the ventral ACC integrates emotion and conflict and prioritizes the processing of conflict in emotional trials. This adaptive mechanism ensures rapid detection and resolution of conflict in potentially threatening situations signaled by emotional stimuli. Hum Brain Mapp, 2011. © 2010 Wiley‐Liss, Inc.
